doc.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Skin-color casting: Volkswagen ad and the Snader film
summary: Milt Hinton replaces Barksdale for the ad; Marshal Royal replaces DeFranco on the Basie film; laughing to keep from crying.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: You were talking about the Volkswagen commercial where – I think Jimmie Crawford was in that?

Yeah, Cleve. Yeah, man, that was way back. I couldn’t remember. When you list the people, I can remember them now. Snooky, me, Cleve, Craw, Ernie. There were 10 of us. I can’t believe that all 10 got out of there playing instruments. But we did the music, and then we got ready to film, and the cats said, oh no. We can’t do this, because we have to have somebody whose more ethnically in line with the rest of it.

Absolutely. Yeah. So, the way Milt Hinton got on it, Milt took Barksdale’s place as a guitar player. Milt’s a bass player, you know, but he came out with the banjo or something. But he was darker skinned, of course, than Barksdale, and Barksdale
couldn’t make the gig. This is the same thing in reverse when we did the thing with Basie for the Snader Productions. Remember that?

We were doing a film with Count Basie and Billie Holiday and Sugar Chile Robinson. The band was Basie, Gus Johnson, Freddie Green, Wardell Gray, me, and Jimmie Lewis. Buddy DeFranco was in the band. Buddy DeFranco – we got ready to film at Snader Productions in Hollywood . . .
Oh, this is why – how the other gentleman came in – Marshal came in . . .
How did – what did you say amongst yourselves when something came – did you laugh about it? Were you angry about it? How did you react to that kind of thing?

You reach the point, Bill, after so many years of being subjected to that kind of indignity, ’til you had to laugh at it. That’s the way we learned from the slaves. That’s the way the cakewalk was born. That’s the way . . .
Laugh, yeah. Laugh to keep from crying. We just – what can you do about it? You get mad enough to kill. There’s no point in killing. You got to hang in there and make it work.
